title: Local Universality and Structural Certificates for Minimal Fixed-Depth Two-Qutrit Gate Decomposition
authors: Yurui Liu, Ruoting Dou, Peng Xu, Xinsheng Tan, Shengjun Wu, Yang Yu, Zeng-Bing Chen
abstract: We study a dimension-saturating fixed-core ansatz in which four copies of a fixed, non-tunable two-qutrit core $K\in SU(9)$ are interleaved with five adjustable local layers from $L=SU(3)\otimes SU(3)$. Since $\dim SU(9)=80$ and $5\dim L=80$, this is the shortest fixed-core architecture not excluded by parameter counting. We formulate the smooth map $Φ_K:L^5\to SU(9)$ and use its right-trivialized differential to give verifiable certificates for local universality. We construct an explicit Clifford-word core whose Pauli-label splitting makes the identity-point differential an exact isometry, and we classify all 2304 symplectic actions satisfying the same splitting criterion. We also prove a structural obstruction for an important symmetry class: every complex-symmetric core $K=K^{T}$, including every core generated by a time-independent real-symmetric Hamiltonian in the chosen computational basis, has identity-point differential rank at most 78; hence any full-rank certificate for such a core must occur away from that point. We then assess a hardware-motivated superconducting core generated by a noncommuting, temporally asymmetric drive. Direct calculation verifies $K_{\rm sc}\neq K_{\rm sc}^{\mathsf T}$, and the core achieves $F_{\rm avg}\ge 0.999$ for all 1000 Haar-random targets tested under the stated restart protocol. We also report favorable sampled Jacobian-rank, structured-target, and robustness diagnostics. These results establish local universality at the parameter-counting-minimal, dimension-saturating depth, with an exact Clifford certificate complemented by a hardware-motivated numerical case study. Throughout, we separate exact local certificates from numerical evidence for broader synthesis performance.
summary: This paper rigorously proves local universality for decomposing two-qutrit gates by constructing a parameter-counting-minimal ansatz and deriving an exact mathematical certificate via differential analysis. It contrasts this theoretical proof with practical hardware testing using superconducting cores, demonstrating high fidelity while respecting structural constraints imposed by gate symmetries.
main_problem: The primary goal is determining local universality for decomposing fixed-depth quantum gates acting on two qutrits ($SU(9)$). This involves finding structural certificates proving that the gate set can approximate any target gate within a certain fidelity.
main_result: Local universality is established using an exact Clifford certificate derived from a parameter-counting-minimal, dimension-saturating ansatz. The study also identifies a structural obstruction for complex-symmetric cores and validates performance with a hardware-motivated core ($K_{sc}$).
method: The authors use differential geometry on the gate decomposition map $\Phi_K$, employing the right-trivialized differential to derive local certificates of full rank (local surjectivity). They complement this theory with numerical benchmarking using superconducting circuit models.
model_or_system: The system is a two-qutrit quantum gate space, $SU(9)$. The ansatz uses four fixed copies of a core $K \in SU(9)$ interleaved with five adjustable local layers from $L=SU(3)\otimes SU(3)$.
key_observables: Local differential rank (must equal 80 for universality), average fidelity ($F_{	ext{avg}} \ge 0.999$), and the minimum singular value ($\sigma_{\min}$) of the Jacobian matrix.
important_parameters: The dimension saturation condition ($5 \cdot \dim L = \dim SU(9) = 80$) is crucial; the perturbation amplitude $\epsilon$ was tested up to $0.20$.
main_assumptions: The results strictly prove *local* universality, and global surjectivity remains an open question. The numerical diagnostics are interpreted as sampled evidence rather than analytic guarantees.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the dimension-saturating four-core ansatz structure; Figure 10 benchmarks structured targets (CZ, CNOT, etc.) for the superconducting core $K_{sc}$ under fixed-budget synthesis.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using differential geometry and provides an exact Clifford certificate. It then analyzes structural obstructions related to symmetry ($K=K^T$). Finally, it validates these findings by applying the theory to a hardware-motivated superconducting core ($K_{sc}$) through numerical testing of fidelity under perturbation.
why_interesting: This work bridges abstract quantum information theory (local universality proofs) with concrete physical implementations using superconducting qudits. The explicit handling of structural constraints based on symmetry is highly relevant for designing robust, physically realizable quantum circuits.

Panel (a) shows the distribution of the sampled pointwise smallest singular value σmin(Apt); the smallest recorded value, 4.08 × 10−9, lies well above the numerical rank floor, so no sampled rank collapse occurs. Panel (b) shows high-precision Haar-random synthesis for one randomly selected good Clifford-word core. The dashed line marks Favg = 1 −10−10.

FIG. 3. Hamiltonian-parameter robustness under shared static coefficient offsets. (a) Perturbed-core recompilation. The nonzero Hamiltonian coefficients are varied multiplicatively along 20 fixed offset directions, while nominally zero coefficients are held at zero. The complete dense scan reuses these directions at each of 14 sampled amplitudes through ϵ = 0.20. Each perturbed core is evaluated on the same 100-target subset, and success means Favg ≥0.999. The line is the median core-wise success fraction, the dark band is the interquartile range, the light band is the 5th–95th percentile range, and faint lines show individual core directions. Panel (a) shows the distribution of σmin(Apt); the smallest recorded value is 4.08 × 10−9, so no sampled configuration reaches the numerical rank floor. Panel (b) shows the distribution of log10(v5,eff). Both panels are finite-precision sampled diagnostics rather than uniform bounds over L5.

FIG. 5. Fold-like diagnostics for the Clifford-word core. Left, a representative singular-value spectrum of MKCl(hbad) shows one near-zero singular value at the numerical floor and a visible gap to σ2. Right, a finite-difference scan along the approximate right-null direction, projected onto the left-null direction, is well fit by a quadratic curve. These finite-precision diagnostics are numerically consistent with simple-fold behavior; they are not an interval-certified fold proof.
